tagline: Fifty states from ocean to ocean
overview:
The United States stretches across the middle of North America from the Atlantic to the Pacific, plus Alaska in the far northwest and the Hawaiian islands in the Pacific. Covering about 9.4 million km², it is among the largest countries in the world, bordering Canada and Mexico and spanning six main time zones.

About 335 million people live in the United States, the third most of any country. English is the main language, though Spanish is spoken by tens of millions and hundreds of other languages are heard in its cities. Washington, D.C. is the capital; New York, Los Angeles and Chicago are the biggest cities.

The country is a federal republic of fifty states, each with its own laws and government, under an elected president and Congress. Its films, music, universities, technology companies and sports have influence far beyond its borders, and it has long been shaped by people arriving from everywhere.
landAndNature: Almost every landscape on Earth appears somewhere in the United States. The Appalachian Mountains roll down the east; the flat interior grows corn and wheat across the Great Plains; the Rocky Mountains rise in the west, followed by deserts and the Sierra Nevada. The Mississippi River drains a basin covering much of the country. The Grand Canyon cuts 1,800 meters into Arizona rock, Yellowstone sits atop a supervolcano and holds half the world's geysers, and California's giant sequoias are the largest trees alive. Alaska has grizzly bears and glaciers; Hawaii has active volcanoes and reefs. Tornado Alley in the center sees more tornadoes than anywhere else on the planet, and hurricanes strike the Gulf and Atlantic coasts.
peopleAndCulture: American culture is a mixture built from Indigenous nations, European settlers, Africans brought in slavery, and waves of immigrants from Asia, Latin America and beyond. That mix gave the world jazz, blues, country, rock and roll and hip-hop, all rooted in African American musical traditions. Hollywood films and American television travel everywhere. Baseball, basketball, American football and ice hockey fill enormous stadiums, and basketball was invented here in 1891. Thanksgiving in November brings families together over turkey; July 4 marks independence with fireworks. Food ranges from Texas barbecue and New Orleans gumbo to New York bagels and Californian tacos. The National Park System, begun with Yellowstone in 1872, was among the world's first efforts to protect wild land for everyone.
history: Hundreds of Indigenous nations lived across the continent for thousands of years, from the Haudenosaunee in the east to the Lakota on the plains and the Navajo in the southwest. English colonies grew along the Atlantic from 1607, and thirteen declared independence in 1776. As the country expanded west, Indigenous peoples were pushed off their lands by treaty and force; the Cherokee and other southeastern nations were driven west in the 1830s on the Trail of Tears, where thousands died. Millions of enslaved Africans worked southern plantations until the Civil War of 1861–1865 ended slavery. Segregation laws followed, and the civil rights movement of the 1950s and 1960s, led by figures such as Martin Luther King Jr. and Rosa Parks, overturned them. The country emerged from World War II as a superpower and landed astronauts on the Moon in 1969.
funFacts: Alaska is so wide that it holds both the westernmost and easternmost points of the country, crossing the date line.
Yellowstone, established in 1872, was the world's first national park and sits above a supervolcano.
The Library of Congress holds well over 170 million items, making it the largest library in the world.
Hawaii's Big Island keeps growing as lava from Kilauea flows into the sea and hardens into new land.
The United States has no official national language at the federal level, though English is used in government.
A bristlecone pine in California's White Mountains has been alive for more than 4,800 years, older than the pyramids of Giza.
